newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rains good for Porgera but fail to help Ok Tedi.
newsitem.headline: Rains good for Porgera but fail to help Ok Tedi.

text.p: Light rains that have enabled the Porgera gold mine in Papua New Guinea's highlands region to resume partial milling operations have not been enough to restart the Ok Tedi copper and gold mine located 210 km to the east, the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd said on Thursday.
"Our operations remained halted," a BHP spokesman for OK Tedi told Reuters from Port Moresby.
Rains tend to fall in isolated areas in the central highlands rather than over wide areas, the spokesman said.

The partners in the Porgera mine said earlier on Thursday that recent rainfall had made it possible to restart milling at half capacity of 7,000 tonnes of ore a day for one week following an 18-day shut down.
The Ok Tedi mine produces about 600,000 tonnes of concentrate a year.

It has long term supply contracts with Germany's Norddeutsche Affinerie, Finland's Outokumpu Oy, Philippines Associated Smelting and Refining Corp (PASAR), South Korea's LG Metals Corp, Mitsui & Co Ltd and the Japanese Smelter Pool which consists of seven Japanese smelters.

BHP said earlier on Thursday a declaration of force majeure was not currently being considered and that BHPwas keeping in contact with customers around the world, who have agreed to adjust their shipping schedules during the drought.
The mine, located in PNG's western province, was forced last Sunday to shut the second of two semi-autogenous grinding mills after reviewing supplies of diesel fuel
The mine's other mill was shut a week earlier as a result of the dry weather spell affecting the country's highlands region.
BHP owns 52.6 percent of the mine. The other partners are Canada's Inmet Mining Corp with 17.4 percent and the remainder held by the PNG government.

The partners in the Porgera joint venture are operator Placer Dome Inc with 50 percent, 25 percent shareholder Goldfields Ltd, the PNG government-controlled Orogen Minerals Ltd with 15 percent and the government of Papua New Guinea with 10 percent.
